1:
Gill reconstructs the movement behind the opening verb. After making the covenant he was directed to make, Moses dismissed the people to their tents and went to his own; now he returns, having ordered them to meet him again, probably at the tabernacle — with which the Targum of Jonathan agrees in saying he went to the tabernacle of the house of doctrine. Aben Ezra reads it otherwise, that he went to each tribe as they lay encamped, to tell them he was about to die and to strengthen their hearts, that they might not be afraid. Calvin asks why addresses so far from gratifying, full of threats and reproofs, had to be heard from Moses' own mouth: had they been delivered after his death, the people would straightway have exclaimed that they were devised by someone else and his name falsely attached to them. The moment added weight of another kind: we know with what attention the last words of the dying are received, and Moses, with one foot already raised to go where God called him, spoke as bidding them a final farewell, so that to the dignity of the prophetic office was added the force of a testamentary disposition.

On the hundred and twenty years Clarke notes that the lawgiver's life was exactly the length of time Noah employed in preaching righteousness to the antediluvian world, and divides it into three periods of forty: forty years in Egypt in Pharaoh's court, acquiring the learning and wisdom of the Egyptians; forty in Midian in preparation for his mission; and forty guiding Israel under the express authority of God. Keil guards the first of the two reasons against the later statement that Moses' eye was not dim nor his natural force abated: that is merely an affirmation that he retained the ability to see and to work to the last moment of his life, which by no means precludes his noticing the decline of his strength and feeling death approach. Calvin presses the same question harder: Moses would not have been useless because his eyes were dim or his members tremulous, but because his age no longer allowed him to perform his usual duties; he had been preternaturally preserved until then, but having reached the end of his course it was necessary that he should suddenly sink. To go out and come in is equivalent to performing the functions of life, as David is said to have done at Saul's bidding. Wesley glosses it more narrowly as performing the office of a leader or governor.

Henry hears reluctance in the repeated farewells: Moses was loth to part, not because he was loth to go to God but because he was loth to leave them, fearing that when he had left them they would leave God. Though Joshua was continued to fight for them in the valley, they would want Moses to intercede on the hill as at Rephidim; and the sentence that he should not go over Jordan put a full stop to his usefulness — hitherto he must serve, but no further. Henry knows no reason why any of us should desire to live longer than while God has work for us to do. Calvin draws the general lesson from the naming of a successor. Whenever God raises up men endowed with excellent gifts He so uses their labours for a time as still to retain others in His hand; His power is not tied to the illustrious qualities of men, as though their death were His destruction. Joshua is not obtruded on Moses' own authority but declared to be called by God, the people bidden to remember what had long ago been revealed. Keil states the promise plainly: the Lord would go before Israel and destroy the Canaanites as He had the two kings of the Amorites, Israel's part being to do to them as commanded.
4:
Calvin reads the appeal to Sihon and Og as an argument from experience: as God had delivered the two Amorite kings into their hands, so He would give the same success against the rest, for though the world is subject to many revolutions God remains like Himself, His counsel never changed and His power never diminished. By such a proof he encourages their expectations, and exhorts them to execute the command resolutely — to purge the land of Canaan by the destruction of its inhabitants. In appearance, Calvin grants, this was fierce and cruel, to leave not one alive; but since God had justly devoted them to extinction, it was not lawful for Israel to inquire what was to be done, but to abandon all discussion and obey. That they spared many made their remissness the worse, since God had often prepared them to execute the vengeance He had decreed. Gill notes that where the Lord is said to give them up before Israel's face, the Targum of Jonathan reads the Word of the Lord shall deliver them up.

On the charge to be strong Clarke observes that the verb is the one used in Exodus for the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, and that the Septuagint renders both this verse and the next play the man and be strong — whence St. Paul seems to have borrowed his words to the Corinthians: stand firm in the faith, play the man, be vigorous. Gill turns the same Greek into being strong in the Lord and in the power of his might, relying on him that goes before. Calvin fastens instead on the promise attached to the command. The people were animated to perseverance of hope by God's declaring that He would be their helper even to the end, and by that lesson, he says, the hallucination is refuted whereby theologians deny that believers can be certain of God's grace except as to their present state, holding faith in suspense so that we believe only for a day, uncertain what God will do with us on the morrow. If faith corresponds with God's promises, it must extend itself to our whole life and beyond death itself, for God removes all doubt as to the future by saying, I will not leave thee nor forsake thee.

That Moses turns from the nation to one man Calvin takes as evidence that a public charge needs a twofold confirmation. It is more difficult to lead all the rest than to follow a leader, so he who is set over many should far excel them; and since in proportion to his honour a man disdainfully looks down on all admonition, Moses overthrows that fastidiousness by showing that those in authority must not only be instructed with the others but even more urgently dealt with. The fear forbidden here is not feeling but its mastery: Calvin will not have them so deprived of sense as to be hardened into indifference to danger, or suppose with certain madmen that there is no bravery without stupidity, but possessed of a confidence that overcomes the fears which impede their calling. Keil defends the received reading of the promise to Joshua, thou wilt come with this people into the land: the emendation that would make it thou wilt bring, after a later verse, is an unnecessary conjecture, since Joshua is not appointed leader here but simply promised an entrance with all the people. Clarke takes the four clauses of the last verse one by one — He will go before thee, to prepare thy way; be with thee in all thy journeys and enterprises; not fail thee, for thy expectation cannot be too large; not forsake thee, since without Him thou canst do nothing, and He will continue with thee in such a manner that the excellence of the power shall appear to be of Him and not of man.
9:
What Moses wrote is disputed among the commentators in a narrow range. Gill takes this law for the book of Deuteronomy, or else the whole Pentateuch, the five books which taken together are sometimes so called; Henry reports that Bishop Patrick understood all five, supposing that though Moses had written most of them before, he did not finish till now and here put his last hand to that sacred volume, while many take it of Deuteronomy alone, this grand abridgment of the law, the discourses which have taken up the whole book and which he, being divinely inspired in them, wrote as the word of God. Henry gives two reasons for the writing: that those who had heard it might often review it themselves and call it to mind, and that it might be the more safely handed down to posterity. The church has received abundance of advantage from the writing as well as the preaching of divine things, for faith comes not only by hearing but by reading; and the same care taken of the law, he adds, was taken of the gospel, which soon after it was preached was written, that it might reach those on whom the ends of the world are come.

Clarke rejects one rabbinic tradition and accepts another. That Moses wrote thirteen copies, one for each of the twelve tribes and a thirteenth to be laid up by the ark, deserves little credit; that he wrote two is likely, since the law was properly a covenant or contract between God and the people, and it is natural to suppose each contracting party had one. The copy laid beside the ark was the Lord's, kept as a standard for reference and a witness against the people should they break it or become idolatrous; the copy given to the priests and Levites was the people's, for general use. Calvin infers a standing duty from the mere fact of the deposit. Though it is only related that the Levites were commanded to recite the book every seventh year, it would have been absurd that the Law should lie buried seven whole years together and not a word of its instruction be heard; the difficulty of hearing in so great a multitude was great, and the recollection would soon have vanished. They were appointed rather as guardians of the Law, that the people might daily inquire of them the right way of serving God, and that they might bring forward in due season whatever was profitable to know.

In this Calvin sees represented as in a mirror what Paul calls the Church, the pillar and ground of the truth: purity of doctrine is preserved unimpaired and propagated by the ministry of pastors, and piety would soon decay if the living preaching of doctrine should cease — whence Paul also charges Timothy to commit sound doctrine to faithful men, who should be able to teach others also. The naming of the elders beside the priests is not superfluous. Calvin makes them coadjutors rather than teachers, given to uphold the doctrine of the Law and not suffer it to be scorned, since we know how great is the insolence of the people in rejecting pious teachers unless those in authority restrain them. Wesley reads the charge to the priests as the practical half of the same thing: they were to keep it carefully and religiously, bring it forth upon occasion, read it, and instruct the people out of it. Henry draws the further inference from the elders' inclusion, that magistrates by their power, as well as ministers by their doctrine, are to maintain religion and take care that the law be neither broken nor lost.
10:
Clarke explains the choice of the sabbatical year by the temper it produced: in the year of release the people's minds, under a peculiar degree of solemnity, were better disposed to hear and profit by the words of God — and on that ground he takes the whole book of Deuteronomy to be meant, since it alone contains an epitome of the Pentateuch, as some chief Jewish rabbins also understand the place. Wesley adds that in that year they were freed from debts and worldly cares, and thereby fitter to attend on God's service. Keil fixes the occasion: the reading was to fall at the end of every seven years, in the festal season of the year of release, at the feast of tabernacles, when they appeared before the Lord. Clarke then observes that the commandment was rarely attended to. From the first public reading under Joshua to the reign of Jehoshaphat he finds none recorded, a period of five hundred and thirty years; the next was not till the eighteenth year of Josiah, two hundred and eighty-two years later; none other is mentioned till the return from the Babylonish captivity under Nehemiah, and none from then to the destruction of Jerusalem.

Calvin traces the writing itself to the same fear of forgetting. Before this the doctrines of religion had only been expressed by word of mouth, the fathers handing down whatever had been declared to them from heaven, so that faith in Egypt rested only on ancient revelations and their fathers' traditions; but since nothing is easier than for men's minds to forget true doctrine and involve themselves in manifold errors, God consigned the rule of piety to public records, that there might be no pretence of ignorance if their posterity declined from it. The deposit with one tribe he explains by the same knowledge of men: had Moses exhorted all indifferently to read it, scarcely any would have applied themselves, for individuals neglect what is enjoined generally upon all; the Levites are therefore appointed guardians, to watch diligently amidst the neglect of others lest the knowledge of God should fail, and to be its interpreters — as Malachi says the priest's lips should keep knowledge. That such precautions still failed appals him: nothing is too sacred or too well fortified to escape man's wickedness, since with the recitation thus precisely enjoined it was astonishing that the Law should be, as it were, discovered in the time of Josiah, and all aroused by its novelty as if they had never heard of it.

On the summons Gill notes the difference from the other festivals: at the three grand feasts only the males were obliged to appear, women might come but were not bound to it, whereas here all of every age and sex were assembled. Wesley takes both reading and gathering distributively: thou shalt read means thou shalt cause it to be read by the priests or Levites, since he could not read it himself in the hearing of all Israel, and the people were gathered not into one place but into divers assemblies. Calvin will not let the mention of women and children pass as a formality: they are named lest age or sex be pleaded as an excuse, which heightens the dishonesty of those who would debar women as well as children from religious learning, since God invites all into His school. The strangers he understands not of those come into Canaan on business and soon to return home, but of those who had settled and by long residence coalesced into one body with Israel. The stated fruit is that by hearing they might learn to fear God, whence he infers that true religion has its origin in knowledge, and that whatever piety men not instructed by God's word appear to have is mere pretence.
14:
Henry hears in the summons a second warning to a man already prepared. Moses is told again that he must shortly die, for even those most ready to die have need to be often reminded of death's approach; and in consideration of it he must come himself to meet God, since whatever improves our communion with God furthers our preparation for death. He must also bring Joshua to be presented for a successor and to receive his commission; and Moses readily obeys, being not one of those who look with an evil eye upon their successors, but on the contrary rejoicing in him. Gill fixes the time loosely as the same occasion or quickly after, perhaps the same day. Ellicott states what the meeting accomplishes: what Moses had already done before Israel is now ratified by Jehovah to Joshua and to Moses himself.

Ellicott then sets the scene beside two others of the same kind. It may be compared with Aaron and Eleazar going up Mount Hor together, that the priesthood might be transferred from the one to the other, and with Elijah and Elisha crossing Jordan together when Elijah was about to depart. He also marks what closes here: for the last time it is recorded that Jehovah met Moses face to face in the tabernacle, the next meeting being on Mount Nebo, and the next within the veil. Calvin reads the appearance at the door as an act of consecration. Joshua is substituted in the place of Moses by a solemn ceremony, not only that he may be held in greater reverence by men, but that he may be presented before God and so acknowledge himself dedicated to His service; and God's declaring that He will give him a charge is equivalent to saying He will instruct him in his duties. Wesley takes the same clause as issuing directly from God for Joshua's greater encouragement, and to gain him more authority with the people.

On the pillar of cloud the commentators divide the significance between the man and the nation. Calvin holds that the appearance of the glory of God was not less effectual for encouraging Joshua personally than for giving public distinction to his office, since he would never have been recognised as Moses' successor unless this visible approbation had fastened the yoke upon the people. Gill notes only what the sign contained: the Lord appeared as he was wont to do, and in the cloud there was a lustre, a brightness, a glory visible, which showed that he was there. Henry draws a conclusion from the rarity of it. God graciously gives them the meeting, appearing in the tabernacle as the shechinah used to appear; but this is the only time in all this book that we read of the glory of God appearing, whereas we often read of it in the three foregoing books — which perhaps signifies that in the latter days, under the evangelical law, such visible appearances of the divine glory are not to be expected, but that we must take heed to the more sure word of prophecy. He also notes where the blame for the coming breach must lie. If the covenant between God and man be broken, it is man that breaks it, for God never leaves any till they first leave him; and their apostasy is foretold as the effect of their prosperity, since they shall have eaten and filled themselves and waxed fat, security taking off their dread of God's judgments and sensuality inclining them to the idolatries of the heathen. Justly, then, does He cast off those who had so unjustly cast Him off: His providence forsaking them, no longer to protect and prosper, so that they become a prey to their neighbours, and His grace forsaking them, no longer to teach and guide, so that they grow more hardened in their idolatries.
16:
On the euphemism for death Clarke and Calvin pull in different directions. Clarke notes that the Hebrew verb means to lie down, to rest, to take rest in sleep, and metaphorically to die; and he warns that much stress cannot safely be laid on it to prove the immortality of the soul, or that the people in Moses' time had a distinct notion of its separate existence. It was, however, so understood by Jonathan ben Uzziel, whose Targum paraphrases it: thou shalt lie down in the dust with thy fathers, and thy soul shall be laid up in the treasury of the life to come with thy fathers. Calvin takes the same words for consolation on both counts. First the condition of the human race is stated, that Moses may not think it hard to depart from the world like all others, since he was born to this end; but the difference between the death of men and of the brute animals is indicated at the same time, for if our death were total annihilation we should not be said to sleep with our fathers.

Calvin also hears an antithesis between the lying down and the rising up: as soon as Moses has gone to rest, the people's insubordination shall break forth, as though they were released from all laws. Not that this happened at once, for under Joshua they manifested some humility, and the outward form of pure religion was maintained, though soon afterwards they relapsed into their old habits; and perhaps the admonition served as a preventive, that they should not fall away so soon. He then counts the aggravations of the crime foretold. They would be led away not only into the superstitions learnt in Egypt but into the defilements of Canaan, which God had willed should be purged by their own hand — far more disgraceful to embrace the false gods of a people whose conquerors and judges they were than to invent fresh idols; and they would desert the God who had adopted them, without pretence of ignorance, having been again and again so solemnly warned. Whoever turn aside to superstitious worship are covenant breakers, and vain are the pretences of all who profess to worship the supreme God together with idols. Wesley finds a further folly in the object of the worship: the strangers of the land are the Canaanites, turned out of their possessions and become strangers in their own land, so that Israel would serve gods which could neither preserve their friends nor annoy their enemies.

Against the broken covenant Ellicott sets a promise in identical Hebrew, the angel's word at Bochim, I said, I will never break my covenant with you, and beside it the apostle's rule that if we believe not, yet He abideth faithful, for He cannot deny Himself. Gill measures the kindled anger by the nearest human likeness: it is as the anger of a man against a wife who has treacherously departed from him, and jealousy, the rage of such a man, is very cruel — much more the wrath of a jealous God, who is a consuming fire. Calvin finds a use even in punishment that fails to reform. The first step of prudence is voluntarily to choose what is right, the second to make a stand against evil once admonition has been heard; but if our minds are so blinded that reproofs profit nothing, there is still a third, that those careless in prosperity should at length perceive they are smitten by God's hand and be driven to acknowledge their guilt. Scarcely one in ten of the godly anticipates judgment while God postpones punishment. Wesley and Clarke read the hidden face as the withdrawal of favour, help, approbation and protection, which Clarke takes for the general meaning of the phrase in Scripture; Ellicott cites Rashi, as though I did not see them in their distress.
19:
Why the warning should take the form of a song is answered from antiquity by Clarke and from Israel's later history by Ellicott. Things of great importance were among the ancients put into verse, Clarke says, as the best method of keeping them in remembrance when writing was little practised; even prose was sometimes sung, the history of Herodotus being divided into nine books each inscribed with a Muse's name because they were anciently sung, Homer reported to have sung his poems through the Greek cities, Aristotle observing that the people anciently sung their laws, and Cicero that the Romans sang their heroes' praises at the public festivals. Ellicott adds that the method suited the people better than a written law, since copies could not be multiplied to any great extent, whereas the rhythmical form was easy to retain in memory. He believes Samuel, the first known to have effected anything toward a system of religious education in Israel, used the same means, the earliest companies of prophets being evidently singers and minstrels — whence their influence over Saul — so that in teaching the people historical psalms such as the seventy-eighth and the hundred and sixth, a very efficacious means of spreading the knowledge of God lay in their hands.

Calvin faces the harder question the command raises. It seems absurd that a useless remedy should be applied to an incurable disease: why not rather correct their wickedness and by His Spirit mould their hearts, than pour words in vain into deaf ears? Proud men mock at this way of dealing, as if God were throwing away His labour. But the preaching of the word, though a savour of death to them that perish, is a sacrifice of sweet savour to God, and is not thrown away when it convicts the ungodly and renders them altogether inexcusable; and to some it was profitable unto salvation, for when subdued by chastisement they learnt at length that their iniquities were the source of their evils. On the promise of the good land Calvin marks the aggravation: God will perform to them, unworthy as they are, what He has sworn, and commends the land's fertility because that pledge of His indulgence should have drawn them to love so beneficent a Father — whence their perverseness appears, that when full they would kick against Him, like horses grown intractable from high feeding.

Ellicott takes up the word rendered imagination, used of the thoughts of man's heart before the flood: it is the term commonly used in rabbinical literature for the evil or the good nature in a man, and the nature which they are forming this day would be a literal rendering here — yet God made Balaam say that He had not beheld iniquity in Jacob, and the psalm uses it in saying He knoweth our frame and remembers that we are dust. Wesley glosses it as inclinations to idolatry which they do not check, some not only cherishing it in their hearts but, so far as they dared, secretly practising it. Clarke explains how a song can testify: their general defection is predicted in it, but so as to show how the evil might be avoided, so that if the punishment did come the song would prove they had been sufficiently warned and might have lived to God and escaped. Gill records what Josephus reports of the writing — that Moses set it down in hexameter verse and left it in the sacred book, a prophecy of things future according to which all things have been done and are done, in nothing erring from the truth. Henry notes the order of publication: he wrote it first, as the Spirit of God indited it then spoke it in the ears of all the congregation and taught it, that is, gave out copies and ordered the people to learn it by heart.
23:
Who speaks the charge to Joshua is a real question, and Gill works through it. The connection favours Moses, the nearer antecedent of the pronoun, and the Septuagint translators so understood it — but they were then obliged to alter what follows, reading the Lord sware for I sware, and he shall be with thee for I will be with thee. Aben Ezra reaches the same sense without departing from the genuine reading, by supposing Moses gave the charge in the name and by the authority of the Lord. Gill judges it best to understand the Lord himself as the speaker, since it was He who ordered the two to present themselves before Him for this very purpose, and the following clauses best agree with Him. Ellicott says what is new in the moment: this is the first record of God's direct communion with Joshua, who had been with Moses on the mount during the first forty days and departed not out of the tabernacle when they came down, yet of whom no divine communication apart from Moses is noted before this.

By the words of this law Calvin understands not only this book but the other three, and finds an implied antithesis between the two tables written by God's hand and the exposition afterwards added, lest there should be obscurity about God's will from the brevity with which it was delivered. Since the mind of man is inclined to vanity and led away by its levity, and has besides the faults of inquisitiveness, audacity in invention and love of novelty, religion would have been corrupted a thousand ways had not its rule been written down for posterity — the more so, he adds, as the books of Moses were for a long time buried through the carelessness of people and priests. Wesley explains the deposit: the book lay outside, in a little chest fixed to the ark, since nothing but the tables of stone were contained within, and kept there for greater security and reverence; and he guesses it was the very copy which, after being some way misplaced, was found in the house of the Lord in the days of Josiah and read publicly by the king himself, against a people then almost ripe for ruin.

Keil reads the next summons as following directly on the handing over: the call to gather was addressed to the very persons to whom Moses had given the book, the elders of all the tribes with the officers, who as the civil authorities of the congregation were collected round him to hear the ode rehearsed. Calvin explains why the law is cited here only as a witness, when it was given rather as the rule of a pious life and a testimony of God's favour: Moses had found the people stiffnecked, and argues from the less to the greater, since if they were rebellious while such a leader lived they would assume greater audacity when he was dead — though he does not arrogate so much as to make their good condition depend on his presence. Clarke turns the same fact toward the reader. Never was a people more fully warned, and from that we may see they were under no fatal constraining necessity to sin; they might have avoided it, but would not. Those who abuse God's grace shall not only have it taken from them but be punished for the abuse as well as the transgression, since every sin is double — grace resisted and transgression committed — and God will visit for both. Henry ends where Moses does, with the plain word that after his death they would utterly corrupt themselves: many a sad thought it cost him, but his comfort was that he had done his duty and that God would be glorified in their dispersion if not in their settlement, for the foundation of God stands sure.
28:
Moses seems to contradict himself, Calvin observes, when he commands only the elders and the officers to be called to listen, and then records that he recited the song to the whole congregation. The two are easily reconciled from the order he was accustomed to observe in gathering the multitude: it is manifest from many passages that they were not called together promiscuously, but that the heads of tribes and the princes of the people each led their own band, so that the assembling of the elders here, far from excluding the rest, rather indicates that the whole people were gathered by their tribes and classes. The context confirms it, for he assuredly did not call heaven and earth to record against the officers only; under the leaders the whole multitude is included. Gill reaches the same place from the other side: the words were spoken not in the hearing of every individual of that vast body — no man could be heard by so numerous a congregation — but in the hearing of their heads and representatives, the elders of the tribes and the officers ordered to gather for this purpose, by whom he understands the princes and all other inferior magistrates.

On the tone of the address Calvin is candid about what it cost. It was the perverse nature of the people which extorted from Moses that unmixed bitterness with which he speaks to them again; doubtless he would have desired to leave a pleasing recollection of himself, and would willingly have exhorted them to their duties with blandness or at any rate with placidity, but their stubbornness compelled him to testify his indignation in the severity of his address. Nor does he judge from conjecture what they would do: he expressly declares that he knew it for certain, unquestionably because the Spirit, in dictating the song, had also informed him of it. Gill likewise takes the foreknowledge to be prophetic, and dates the falling away not immediately after the death now at hand but some time after it. Calvin then reads the manner of the corruption out of the words themselves. They would depart from the way which they had learned; and since their perfect soundness lay in obeying God and following the way He showed them, it was by forsaking the law that they were corrupted — in which Moses indirectly reproves their ingratitude, as one who had thrown away his labour upon such despisers of pious instruction.

The recitation was therefore meant to work after the event. Calvin says Moses desired the song to be sung by them so that when afflicted and half consumed by miseries they might at last learn that God is a just avenger — the advantage being that those whose state was not altogether desperate should return to their senses, while the reprobate should be more and more condemned. Ellicott examines the phrase in the latter days, a not uncommon prophetical expression used with considerable latitude, which occurs for the first time in Jacob's blessing and again in Balaam's oracle and earlier in this book; some would refer it to the days of the Messiah and make it almost a technical term, but a comparison of these few passages shows that it cannot be tied strictly to any one period. Keil marks the last verse as the introduction to the rehearsal of the ode, and Ellicott closes the chapter with a symmetry: the exodus of Israel begins and ends with a song of Moses. The song at the Red Sea is the one usually so called, and is commonly thought to be the song of Moses named in the Revelation; but Ellicott points to the remarkable resemblance between that passage and the opening lines of the song which is about to follow here.
